comparator.sourceNotes: Verified current 2026–2027 regulatory framework from the actual official 32-page OER (effective 1 September 2026), visually compared with extracted text. Articles 3.4–3.6, pages 12–16: eight 15-EC blocks in years 1–2, 25-EC free choice, 15-EC Choices and Dilemmas and 20-EC graduation = 180 unique EC; K/AVV/integration submodules are children and not additional credits. PPO is pass/fail without separate EC in this framework. Article 4.1 and 8.1 require positive first-year BSA for later-year blocks; normally 60 EC plus PPO with article 3.5 first-year compensation (one 5.0–5.4 compensated by another module at least 6.0). No between-module compensation in years 2–3. Graduation entry requires all B1/B2 components and a timely secured placement; the three GW310/GW311/GW312 codes represent alternative start trajectories for one 20-EC project, not cumulative projects. Free choice permits approved minors/electives/exchange/international placement under article 3.6; outside LDE universities needs examination-board permission requested at least eight weeks in advance; exchange needs board-approved non-overlapping on-campus formally assessed courses, at least half B2 level, minimum 25 EC; international placements of 10/15 EC need coordinator approval. Required mentoring/coaching/intervision and stated participation requirements are non-credit obligations. Honours is extracurricular. Appendix 1, page 31, explicitly starts the redesigned curriculum in 2027–2028: free choice changes from 25 to 30 EC, graduation from 20 to 30 EC and Block 9 from 15 to zero. The public programme page’s 30 EC therefore is not imported into the retained 2026–2027 framework. This is a year-specific regulatory snapshot, not a guarantee that a new entrant will retain unchanged rules throughout three future years. No visible/hidden text disagreement was found on the inspected current and future tables.

alternatives.concept: A population-health programme combines epidemiology, medical and health psychology, lifespan development and disease mechanisms with statistics, qualitative research and research synthesis. Economics, accounting, organisational psychology, public institutions, rights and ethics provide complementary tools for understanding collective choices and organisations. AI Ethics directly considers confidentiality, responsibility and trust in clinical and therapeutic settings. The programme sustains study of health and illness; its general legal, economic and management courses do not become Dutch health-system, health-insurance or patient-law training.

alternatives.concept: This health-and-society programme centres epidemiology, health and abnormal psychology, lifespan development, youth resilience, psychological assessment concepts and research synthesis. Sociology, qualitative methods, public economics, organisations, rights and ethics support inquiry into health needs, social conditions and collective choices. AI Ethics adds a direct examination of clinical confidentiality and children’s interactions with AI. Psychological assessment and psychotherapy are studied academically; the programme does not provide clinical care training or the external degree’s integrated youth-service and healthcare-policy practice.

alternatives.distinctnessRationale: The programmes share 18 courses, with 6 different courses (45 EC) in each. The closest adds biological/disease science, accounting, microeconomics and econometrics; the related programme adds social and abnormal psychology, youth resilience, assessment/psychotherapy concepts, modern sociology and constitutional comparison. Their organising questions differ between population/institutional analysis and development, mental health and social conditions across the lifecourse.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Semester 1 establishes epidemiology, economics, law and sociology; semester 2 adds PPD, general research/statistics, brain/behaviour and qualitative methods. Semester 3 introduces biological foundations, multivariate statistics, human rights and comparative politics. Semester 4 adds economics, lifespan development and evidence synthesis. Semester 5 combines health psychology, organisations, accounting and social theory. The final semester adds econometrics, ethics, mechanisms of disease and AI ethics. The biological gateway precedes disease mechanisms, the psychology gateway precedes dependent psychology, and the methods gateway precedes dependent economics/organisational courses. Every assigned offering and formal prerequisite is independently checked.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Two programmes survive the course-content challenge. The original markets option had no health course and depended on relabelling generic economics, global business and leadership as healthcare teaching. Adding the necessary health-science anchor and retaining relevant economic/organisational tools converges on the closest programme; residual business specialisation does not establish a substantively distinct healthcare-markets curriculum. The lifecourse option sustains actual health/developmental content and differs meaningfully from the closest. A separate healthcare-innovation programme is not established by generic business innovation or technical/image-analysis courses: these do not teach the external organisational implementation and service-design enquiry. Its clinical-AI ethics aspect is retained in both programmes, without claiming a full innovation-design route. No third option is manufactured. The current OER confirms the defining multidisciplinary health-services enquiry and the retained 2026–2027 comparator; its future redesign does not justify a third generic programme.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both directly examine how biological, psychological and social factors shape health, illness and patient experience. Erasmus also integrates legal patient status and questions about health knowledge; UCR concentrates on health psychology.
Both study change across the lifecourse and older age. UCR supplies developmental psychology; Erasmus integrates care needs, ageing and social/organisational/government responses.
Health psychology and youth resilience inform service-user needs, but do not directly deliver the block’s youth-service policy, legal responsibilities, waiting lists and stakeholder project.

Both examine ethical problems raised by data and technology in care. UCR explicitly discusses clinical/therapeutic confidentiality, trust and responsibility in AI; Erasmus addresses a broader set of healthcare dilemmas.
General law and political science do not deliver the Dutch healthcare system’s institutions, financing arrangements and healthcare-specific legal framework.

Both use economic analysis of consumer/provider behaviour, market structures and intervention. UCR teaches general microeconomics; Erasmus specifically studies insurer/provider and insurance markets and their legal rules.

Both directly examine organisational structures, culture, leadership, groups and coordination. UCR supplies general organisational behaviour, while Erasmus integrates healthcare organisations, financial/logistical data and observation.

AI ethics covers an identifiable ethical part of health technology, but is more strongly aligned to Choices and Dilemmas. No included course establishes the complete healthcare innovation/business-case/implementation project.
No scheduled course directly teaches the integrated measurement, improvement, professional regulation and quality governance of healthcare.

The current OER establishes 25 EC of approved minor/elective, exchange or international-placement choice. This has no fixed subject to align; UCR scheduled courses are not presented as a guaranteed approved choice package.

The compulsory 20-EC placement-based independent research/fieldwork project is not delivered by the scheduled research-synthesis seminar. Optional independent research is displayed separately outside the UCR 180 EC; it does not fulfil the required external placement.

notes.text: The UCR programmes combine population health, health psychology and related biological or developmental study with research methods and complementary social, economic, organisational and legal tools. They do not reproduce the Dutch healthcare system, specialist health law, healthcare quality/insurance framework or the required organisation-based research placement.

audience.programmeDescription: Health Sciences, Policy & Management of Healthcare at Erasmus studies health services through economics, law, social-medical science, public policy, organisations and ethics. Its Dutch-taught, full-time BSc combines thematic study with research and practical projects.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option combines population health, health psychology, development and disease science with research methods and complementary study of institutions, economics and organisations. The second centres health needs and social conditions across the lifecourse, including mental health and youth. Both offer substantial health-focused study with a different emphasis from Erasmus’s integrated healthcare-policy and management degree. They do not reproduce specialist Dutch health-system, insurance, health-law or quality training, or the required research placement. Shared rows show meaningful partial relationships; blank cells preserve other content and gaps.

curriculum.limitation: This shows the 2026–2027 framework. A redesigned curriculum starts in 2027–2028, so check the official regulations for the rules applying to your year. Free-choice subjects remain open within approved options.

componentNotes.y1-dutch-system: First-year blocks include knowledge, academic skills and integration projects, with a pass/fail development strand. Progression normally requires all 60 first-year EC and this strand, subject to the first-year compensation rules.
componentNotes.y3-free-choice: 25 EC of permitted minors/electives, exchange or international placement. Outside-university choices and exchange require approval; relevant entry rules apply. The urban public-health minor is an optional possibility, not a compulsory pathway.
componentNotes.y3-graduation: One compulsory 20-EC research placement and project. Entry requires all first- and second-year components and a secured placement. September and February start codes are alternatives.
